detail:

BofA lowered its price target on Axsome to $264 from $276 but maintained a 'Buy' rating, representing an 85% upside potential.

TD Cowen analyst Joseph Thome reiterated a 'Buy' rating with a $135 price target, calling shares 'significantly undervalued.'

Axsome reported a 52% surge in Q3 revenue to $259.7 million, above estimates of $249.2 million, according to Fiscal.ai

Shares of Axsome Therapeutics (AXSM) have declined nearly 20% over the past month, but Wall Street believes the selloff may be excessive despite concerns surrounding the company's Alzheimer's disease agitation treatment launch.

AXSM stock was up 5% at the time of writing, having fallen to a 52-week low in the previous session.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

BofA Still Sees Significant Upside

BofA lowered its price target on Axsome to $264 from $276 but maintained a 'Buy' rating, according to The Fly. The updated price target still implies a roughly 85% upside from current levels.

The firm said that while Axsome's third-quarter (Q3) results were largely in line with expectations, investors remain concerned about the pace of the Alzheimer's agitation treatment launch and whether the company can meet full-year 2027 estimates.

BofA said concerns about the slower-than-expected adoption of Axsome's Alzheimer's agitation treatment and its ability to meet full-year 2027 revenue estimates have weighed on shares, but the firm believes the selloff is excessive given the drug's long-term growth potential.

Meanwhile, Baird lowered its price target on Axsome to $220 from $246 and keeps an Outperform rating on the shares.

Axsome's Q3 Revenue Growth Driven By Auvelity Sales

Axsome reported a 52% surge in third-quarter (Q3) revenue to $259.7 million, above estimates of $249.2 million, according to Fiscal.ai. Auvelity drove the growth, with sales up 53% to $207.6 million.

The company reported a loss of $0.25 per share, beating consensus estimates of a $0.64 per-share loss. Axsome ended September with $313.9 million in cash and expects its existing funds to support operations until it becomes cash-flow positive.

Auvelity, an oral medication, was originally approved in 2022 to treat major depressive disorder. In April, 2026, the FDA approved Auvelity for agitation associated with Alzheimer's dementia. Axsome launched the treatment for this new use in June 2026.

With the AI bubble seeming to pop, many people are turning back to legendary old-school investors like Warren Buffett, who has sat through many crashes. Redditors were already calling Berkshire Hathaway a way to protect a portfolio ahead of an AI bubble pop. See why Redditors picked Berkshire. So what would Buffett do today? He could go all in on AI, pile into non-AI stocks, or sit still and ride it out. His recent comments point to the third path, with one AI exception.

At Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting in May, Buffett told CNBC's Becky Quick that the market is not an ideal place to put cash to work, with Berkshire holding close to $400 billion. He said Berkshire picks its spots and sometimes does nothing for long stretches, and that only about five of his 60 years in the business were really juicy. He also said he understands fewer businesses than he did 10 years ago and will not try to beat younger investors who grew up with new technology. He compared the market to a church with a casino attached and called one-day options gambling. The best time to buy, he said, is when nobody answers their phones during a collapse. His only AI comment in that interview was about deep fakes, which he called scary.

In July, Buffett told CNBC that he started Berkshire's bet on Alphabet, a sign he supports the company's big AI spending. He said he was wrong to overlook Alphabet earlier, and that it is more likely to be a winner than 90% or 95% of what Wall Street sells, Bloomberg reported. He did not go all in. He said he likes at least four or five other Berkshire businesses better. Although rate hikes disappeared from the Federal Reserve's playbook for 3 years, Wall Street is preparing for another tightening cycle. Why Rising Rates Fatten Bank Margins

For JPMorgan, Bank of America (NYSE:BAC), Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS) and Citigroup (NYSE:C), the key mechanism is net interest margin: the gap between what a bank earns on loans and securities and what it pays depositors. When the Fed hikes, floating-rate loans reprice higher quickly while many deposit rates lag behind, so the spread widens. That buffer shrinks when savers move cash into higher-paying CDs, when borrowers default, or when bonds bought at lower yields lose value. The pressure ran the other way in the zero-rate era, when 24/7 Wall St. reported that low rates forced banks to re-examine their strategies.

title: Oracle says $20 billion is all it needs, and BofA buys it
detail:
Oracle says $20 billion is all it needs, and BofA buys it
Tobi Opeyemi Amure
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 9:03 PM EST 5 min read
ORCL
BAC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Most of us never see Oracle's name, even when we use it. It sits behind airline bookings, hospital records, and payroll systems, quietly keeping the data straight.

That kind of business usually throws off steady cash. For years, Oracle's did.

I'm clearly not alone in depending on it. Oracle (ORCL) generated $67.4 billion in revenue in fiscal 2026, according to Bank of America's model, and it holds $664 billion in signed contracts it hasn't billed yet, 24/7 Wall St. reported.

"We think that what we're building here is going to create fantastic returns for all of our investors," said Co-CEO Mike Sicilia at the company's investor day on Oct. 28.

However, a subtle shift has emerged in how investors see the bill for that buildout.

According to a Bank of America research report seen by TheStreet, Oracle's funding needs are far smaller than Wall Street feared, which could take the biggest worry off the stock.

Oracle's $20 billion promise cuts the funding fear

At its investor day, Oracle said it needs just $20 billion more to finish its current data center buildout.

"We're announcing that this $20 billion, split evenly between debt and equity, is the final amount needed," said Chief Financial Officer Hilary Maxson.

That means $10 billion of new stock and $10 billion of new debt. It comes on top of a $20 billion stock sale Oracle already completed in its first fiscal quarter, 24/7 Wall St. reported.

The stock jumped 10.7% to $144.54 on Oct. 28. Even after that, it sat about 49% below its 52-week high of $285.46.

Read more: Oracle's 'force majeure' warning lands as AI power gets scarce

Analyst Tal Liani laid out why in a note titled "Analyst day highlights: Focus on funding clarity and growth acceleration."

"Management plans to add 7GW of data center capacity over the next three years across 38 projects, requiring $10bn of equity and 10bn of debt funding, well below Street's ~50bn estimate," wrote Liani.

By my math, that's about $30 billion, or 60%, less outside money than Wall Street had penciled in.

Liani credited "alternative financing, including customer prepayments, vendor financing, and bring-your-own-hardware arrangements." In other words, customers pay upfront, suppliers extend credit, and some clients bring their own chips.

Maxson made the same point. "Customers are willing to make prepayments to preserve the right to receive services from Oracle in the future," she said.

The debt load still matters

Oracle isn't starting from a clean balance sheet.

The company had $125.3 billion in borrowings against $36.4 billion in cash, 24/7 Wall St. reported. Free cash flow was negative $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026 as it spent $55.7 billion on capital projects.

title: Bank of America pulls its Buy on Intel as the comeback slips
detail:
Bank of America pulls its Buy on Intel as the comeback slips
Tobi Opeyemi Amure, Celine Provini
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 7:17 PM EST 5 min read
INTC
BAC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Most people never think about the chip inside their laptop. You pick a brand, a screen size, and a price, and the processor just comes with it.

For decades, that processor was usually made by Intel. That quiet default turned the company into one of the most valuable names in tech.

I'm clearly not alone in owning an Intel machine. Intel (INTC) still sold $8.1 billion of client computing chips, mostly for PCs, in the third quarter alone, out of $16.5 billion in total revenue, according to its earnings release.

The newer engine is the data center. "The resurgence in demand for CPU is a meaningful tailwind for us along our transformation journey," said CEO Lip-Bu Tan on the company's Oct. 29 earnings call.

However, a subtle shift has emerged in how long that transformation might take.

According to a Bank of America research report seen by TheStreet, Intel's turnaround has been pushed out as a collapse in PC shipments and tight chip supply outweigh its booming server business.

Bank of America cuts Intel's target by $45

The headline numbers looked fine at first. Third-quarter revenue rose 21% from a year earlier, and data center sales jumped 78% to $7.3 billion, Intel said.

The outlook did the damage. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, against a consensus of about $17 billion, Yahoo Finance reported. It also expects non-GAAP gross margin to fall to 38% from 44.1%.

"We do not expect a sustained recovery until memory availability improves and pricing begins to normalize," said CFO David Zinsner on the call.

Investors didn't wait. Intel stock fell nearly 29% on Oct. 30, its worst day since 1974, wiping out nearly $140 billion in market value, Yahoo Finance noted.

Related: Intel CEO reveals a PC problem as Goldman cuts stock target

Analyst Vivek Arya downgraded Intel to Neutral from Buy and cut his price target to $100 from $145 in a note titled "Downgrade to Neutral, turnaround pushed out on PC/supply headwinds."

"In our view, the stock has not communicated enough traction with external foundry customers, while its data center strength is offset by a surprisingly sharp drop in PC shipments," wrote Arya.

He expects PC shipments to fall 25% to 30% from the third quarter to the fourth, with "further inventory correction expected in 1H27 [the first half of 2027]."

Bank of America downgraded Intel to Neutral and cut its target to $100 after a massive comeback rally.Maskot / Getty Images
The PC market just had a brutal quarter

Arya isn't guessing about the PC slump. The broader market data says the same thing.

Worldwide PC shipments fell 22.4% from a year earlier to 55.4 million units in the third quarter, according to Gartner data reported by TechEdge AI. IDC counted a 20.1% drop, PC TestBench reported.
